cards.text: Neurons and most glia derive from the {{c1::neuroectoderm}} (neural tube wall).
cards.extra: Origin predicts function.

cards.text: In the PNS (ganglion neurons + Schwann cells), the origin is the {{c1::neural crest}}.
cards.extra: Neural crest also gives melanocytes and adrenal medulla.

cards.text: Which glial cell is the exception, arising from {{c1::mesoderm}} (monocyte lineage)? {{c2::Microglia}}
cards.extra: Hence the resident macrophage of the CNS.

cards.text: Which neuron type has a single axon and multiple dendrites and is the most common (motor, interneuron, Purkinje)? {{c1::Multipolar}}
Which neuron type has one dendrite and one axon at opposite poles? {{c1::Bipolar}}
Bipolar neurons are restricted to the {{c1::retina}}, {{c2::olfactory mucosa}}, and {{c3::cochlear/vestibular ganglia}}.
Which neuron type has one trunk that branches in a {{c1::T}} and is the sensory neuron of the dorsal root ganglion? {{c2::Pseudounipolar}}
cards.extra: Born bipolar; the two processes fuse. True unipolar does not exist in humans.

cards.text: By function, a neuron carrying signals between others (internal bridge, the majority) is an {{c1::interneuron}}.
cards.extra: Afferent = brings in; efferent = sends to effector.

cards.text: The neuron cell body (perikaryon) is the {{c1::trophic}} center; its nucleus is large, spherical, and pale, i.e. {{c2::euchromatic}}, with a prominent nucleolus.
cards.extra: A cell in very high protein synthesis.

cards.text: Which basophilic bodies are rough ER + polyribosomes, staining dark for their {{c1::RNA}}? {{c2::Nissl bodies}}
Nissl bodies are present in the perikaryon and {{c1::dendrites}}, but absent from the {{c2::axon hillock and axon}}.
cards.extra: The practical way to tell a dendrite from an axon on a slide.

cards.text: Which brown pigment accumulates in the aged neuron (lysosomal digestion residue), a sign of age not disease? {{c1::Lipofuscin}}
The neuron's input pole, which tapers, branches, and bears {{c1::spines}} (substrate of plasticity), is the {{c2::dendrite}}.
cards.extra: Contains Nissl.

cards.text: The axon leaves at the {{c1::axon hillock}}, the {{c2::trigger}} zone where the action potential is born.
cards.extra: Uniform caliber, no Nissl.

cards.text: Because the axon makes no protein, it depends on active {{c1::axonal transport}}, running on {{c2::microtubules}} using ATP.
cards.extra: Diffusion alone → years across a 1 m axon.

cards.text: Anterograde axonal transport (body → terminal) uses {{c1::kinesin}}; retrograde (terminal → body) uses {{c2::dynein}}.
Rabies virus and tetanus toxin reach the CNS by the {{c1::retrograde}} route, hijacking {{c2::dynein}}.
cards.extra: Neurotropic via axonal transport, not via blood.

cards.text: At the chemical synapse, the action potential opens {{c1::calcium}} channels in the bouton, and Ca2+ triggers {{c2::vesicle fusion}}.
cards.extra: Neurotransmitter into the cleft → postsynaptic receptors.

cards.text: Which rarer synapse joins cells by {{c1::gap junctions}}, passing ions directly in a {{c2::bidirectional}}, near-instant signal? {{c3::Electrical synapse}}
Which glial cell buffers extracellular {{c1::potassium}}, recycles neurotransmitter, and feeds the neuron {{c2::glucose}}? {{c3::Astrocyte}}
The blood-brain barrier is made by endothelial {{c1::tight junctions}}, induced by the {{c2::astrocyte}} perivascular foot.
cards.extra: Oligodendrocyte myelinates; microglia phagocytoses; only the astrocyte touches the vessel.

cards.text: The {{c1::protoplasmic}} astrocyte (short processes) lives in gray matter; the {{c2::fibrous}} astrocyte (long processes) lives in white matter.
cards.extra: Astrocyte scar after injury = gliosis.

cards.text: CNS myelin is built by the {{c1::oligodendrocyte}} (myelinates several axons at once); PNS myelin by the {{c2::Schwann cell}} (one internode of one axon).
cards.extra: Oligodendrocyte serves many; Schwann serves one.

cards.text: The myelin-free gap rich in {{c1::sodium}} channels where the action potential regenerates, allowing {{c2::saltatory}} conduction, is the {{c3::node of Ranvier}}.
cards.extra: Myelin insulates and forces the signal to jump node to node.

cards.text: A PNS unmyelinated axon is still wrapped by a Schwann cell but {{c1::without a spiral wrap}} (several axons in the cell's grooves).
cards.extra: Schwann around it is not the same as myelin.

cards.text: Which cell is the resident macrophage of the CNS, phagocytosing debris and triggering inflammation on injury? {{c1::Microglia}}
Cells lining the ventricles and central canal are {{c1::ependymal}} cells; over capillaries they specialize into the {{c2::choroid plexus}}, which makes CSF.
Which PNS glial cell wraps the neuron cell bodies inside ganglia, insulating them? {{c1::Satellite cells}}
cards.extra: Unrelated to the muscle satellite cell (a stem cell).

cards.text: Gray matter holds {{c1::cell bodies, dendrites, and synapses}} (neuropil); white matter is {{c2::myelinated axons}}, whose myelin gives the color.
In the cerebral cortex the gray matter lies on the {{c1::outside}}, in {{c2::six}} layers (the basis of Brodmann's map).
The cerebellar cortex has three layers: molecular, {{c1::Purkinje}} (single row of giant cells, the only output), and granular.
In the spinal cord the gray matter lies {{c1::inside}}, in an {{c2::H (butterfly)}} shape.
cards.extra: Cortex gray outside, cord gray inside; no single rule.

cards.text: The three peripheral nerve sheaths are the {{c1::endoneurium}} (each fiber), {{c2::perineurium}} (each fascicle), and {{c3::epineurium}} (whole nerve, with vessels).
cards.extra: Perineurium is also a barrier: its cells have tight junctions.

cards.text: The sensory (dorsal root) ganglion has pseudounipolar neurons and {{c1::makes no synapse}}; the autonomic ganglion has multipolar neurons and {{c2::is a synaptic relay}}.
The meninges, outside in, are {{c1::dura mater}}, {{c2::arachnoid}}, and {{c3::pia mater}}; CSF circulates in the {{c4::subarachnoid}} space.
cards.extra: CSF is made in the choroid plexus and cushions the CNS.
